chapter_title: IPFS and Decentralized Storage for DApps

screens.title: IPFS and Decentralized Storage for DApps
screens.subtitle: Use content addressing to keep large assets off-chain while keeping immutable references on-chain.

narration.text: In this lesson we explore why decentralized storage is essential for DApps and how IPFS provides a practical, content-addressed solution. You will learn what a CID is, why storing large binary files on Ethereum is prohibitive, and how the common pattern stores assets on IPFS while keeping small, immutable references on-chain. We'll use real examples such as uploading an image with a pinning service, obtaining a CID, and then saving an ipfs:// URI in a smart contract. Along the way you will see common pitfalls — relying only on a public gateway, forgetting to pin content, or using mismatched CID versions — and how to avoid them. By the end, you'll understand the trade-offs between pure decentralization and pragmatic reliability, and you will be ready to design a DApp that keeps metadata and media out of expensive on-chain storage while preserving verifiability and availability. Consider how this pattern changes deployment, upgrade, and content moderation strategies in your DApp.

keyIdea.title: Why IPFS?
keyIdea.text: IPFS stores large assets off-chain and returns a content hash (CID). Store only the CID on-chain to keep data verifiable, immutable, and cost-efficient.

screens.title: Why not store large files on-chain?
screens.subtitle: Costs, inefficiency, and the immutable nature of blockchain storage

narration.text: Smart contracts are excellent for logic and small pieces of state, but they are not a general-purpose file store. Storing large binaries directly on Ethereum becomes prohibitively expensive because every byte persisted in contract storage consumes gas paid to validators. Beyond cost, blockchains are optimized for consensus and deterministic execution, not distributed file serving. This leads to inefficiency when serving images, videos, or large JSON metadata. A common misconception is to think that putting data on-chain guarantees permanence without trade-offs. While on-chain storage is durable, it is costly and wastes scarce blockchain resources when used for large assets. The practical pattern is to place large content in a distributed file system like IPFS and store only a tiny, fixed-size reference — typically a CID string — on-chain. For example, an NFT's tokenURI field can hold ipfs://CID. That preserves immutability: the CID itself guarantees the data's integrity, while avoiding excessive gas. In short: use the chain for authoritative references and IPFS for the heavy content. What small piece of state will you keep on-chain in your next DApp? Why not store large files on-chain? means blockchains should store small authoritative references; offload large media to decentralized file systems to keep costs and complexity manageable.. In practical terms, costs, inefficiency, and the immutable nature of blockchain storage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: On-chain is expensive

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › On-chain Limits
Why large files don't belong on-chain
Storing bytes in smart contracts consumes gas, slows transactions, and bloats the chain.
  • Cost: every on-chain byte increases gas and user fees.
  • Performance: blockchains are not optimized for binary serving.
  • Maintainability: updating large on-chain data is expensive and rare.
Common misconception
Storing files on-chain equals permanence. It does, but at a prohibitive cost; permanence can be achieved more cheaply with IPFS plus an on-chain CID reference.
Analogy
Think of the blockchain as a ledger: it records the receipt and the pointer to a warehouse, but not every physical item inside the warehouse. IPFS is the distributed warehouse where large items are stored.
Concrete example
An NFT contract stores ipfs://CID in tokenURI. The image bytes live on IPFS; the chain stores a small string that proves the image contents.
Key Takeaway

Store references on-chain and assets on IPFS to balance permanence and cost.

screens.title: IPFS and Content Addressing
screens.subtitle: How hashing content produces immutable CIDs

narration.text: IPFS is a peer-to-peer distributed file system that uses content addressing rather than location addressing. When you add a file, IPFS cryptographically hashes the file contents; that hash becomes the file's Content Identifier or CID. Because the CID is derived from the content, the same file will always produce the same CID. This property guarantees immutability: if the content changes, it will produce a different CID. A typical CID string looks like an opaque hash; treat it as the canonical fingerprint of that asset. This design brings several practical benefits: nodes can find and serve content from any peer that stores the same CID, content integrity can be verified by re-hashing, and deduplication is automatic — duplicate uploads yield the same CID. A common confusion is to conflate gateways with IPFS itself. Gateways translate ipfs://CIDs into HTTP for browsers but are centralized endpoints. For stronger decentralization, developers can run local IPFS nodes or use client libraries that query peers directly. Remember: CIDs identify content, not location, and that is the key to verifiable, immutable assets in a DApp. IPFS and Content Addressing means a cid is a cryptographic hash of content; identical content yields identical cids and ensures immutability and deduplication.. In practical terms, how hashing content produces immutable cids. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: CID = content fingerprint
keyIdea.text: A CID is a cryptographic hash of content; identical content yields identical CIDs and ensures immutability and deduplication.

How IPFS names content
A file's CID is produced by hashing its bytes. The CID is stable so long as the content is unchanged.
Immutability
CID changes when content changes; content integrity can be validated by re-hashing.
Deduplication
Exact duplicate files produce the same CID, saving storage across the network.
CID example
QmYtnggePQ7rW5j7w6D34nFwQx1VdD1h1c1C1C1C1C1C1C
Gateway vs network

An IPFS gateway exposes content over HTTP but introduces centralization. For resilience, consider pinning or running a node.

Practical note
When designing a DApp, decide whether users rely on public gateways, a dedicated gateway, or direct peer-to-peer retrieval via a node or client library.

screens.title: Typical DApp flow: Upload → CID → On-chain
screens.subtitle: A reliable sequence from file selection to on-chain reference

narration.text: A reliable DApp upload pattern follows a simple sequence: the user selects a file, the DApp uploads it to IPFS or a pinning service, the service returns a CID, and the DApp stores ipfs://CID in a smart contract. First, file selection includes client-side validation such as file type and size limits. Second, the upload can be performed from the browser using a pinning SDK or a backend that holds A P I credentials. Third, once the pinning service returns a CID, the DApp constructs a tokenURI or other reference and submits an on-chain transaction. Fourth, the contract writes a small string or bytes value, minimizing gas. A common pitfall is trying to upload directly from a browser without a stable pinning arrangement — the CID may not be persistently hosted. Another common mistake is storing the full binary as on-chain data rather than the CID. Finally, always confirm the CID after upload and consider adding event listeners or UI feedback for transaction and pinning confirmation. Following this flow keeps your app resilient and auditable while avoiding unnecessary gas costs. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Pitfall

Pro tip

screens.title: Pinning Services vs Running Your Own Node
screens.subtitle: Trade-offs: reliability, cost, and decentralization

narration.text: When you decide how to persist IPFS content, you typically choose between using a pinning service or operating your own IPFS node. Pinning services like Pinata, Web3. storage, or Infura offer convenience: they run reliable infrastructure and expose SDKs so you can pin content quickly from a browser or backend. This is often the recommended path for production DApps because it reduces operational overhead. Running your own node gives you full control and is more decentralized in principle, but it requires uptime, storage management, and understanding of garbage-collection and pin management. A common misconception is that a pinning service is centralized by default. While pinning services are managed by third parties, they still pin content to the IPFS network, and you can combine services or run your own node alongside a service for redundancy. Evaluate costs, SLAs, and trust boundaries: for many DApps, a pinning service plus the ability for power users to run their own nodes strikes a practical balance between availability and decentralization. Pinning Services vs Running Your Own Node means pinning services trade operational burden for availability; running your own node gives control but increases maintenance responsibility.. In practical terms, trade-offs: reliability, cost, and decentralization. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Choose persistence wisely
keyIdea.text: Pinning services trade operational burden for availability; running your own node gives control but increases maintenance responsibility.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Pinning vs Node
Pinning Service
  • Managed infrastructure and SDKs for quick integration.
  • Good availability SLAs and reduced maintenance.
  • Requires trusting a third-party to host pins.
Self-hosted Node
  • Full control over pins and storage policies.
  • Higher operational cost: uptime, backups, disk management.
  • More decentralized in practice if many users run nodes.
Concrete compromise
Use a pinning service for core assets and allow advanced users or partners to run a node and pin content for redundancy. Consider multiple pinning providers for critical assets.
Misconception check
Relying on one public gateway is not the same as pinning. Gateway access and pin persistence are separate concerns.

screens.title: Uploading with Pinata SDK (example)
screens.subtitle: Pin a file and return the IPFS CID from a Node or browser flow

narration.text: This code walkthrough shows how a pinning service SDK can be used to upload a file and return a CID. The example uses the Pinata SDK and explains required keys, typical error handling, and the difference between Node and browser environments. In Node you may use readFileSync or streams, while in a browser you pass a File object. The code checks for A P I key presence and logs an error if keys are missing. When pinFileToIPFS completes successfully, it returns an object with IpfsHash which is the CID. Handle failures by notifying the user and avoid exposing your secret key in client code; prefer a backend when you cannot safely store secrets. Remember to pin with options such as cidVersion when your application requires a specific CID format. Finally, always provide clear UI feedback during upload and when the contract update is in progress. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Pinata SDK
Uploader example
This snippet demonstrates the exact flow used in a Node or browser context when the SDK is available.
// src/utils/ipfs.ts
import pinataSDK from '@pinata/sdk';
import { readFileSync } from 'fs'; // For Node.js environment, use File object in browser

const pinataApiKey = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_PINATA_API_KEY;
const pinataSecretApiKey = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_PINATA_SECRET_API_KEY;

const pinata = new pinataSDK(pinataApiKey, pinataSecretApiKey);

export async function uploadFileToIPFS(file: File): Promise {
  if (!pinataApiKey || !pinataSecretApiKey) {
    return null;
  }

  try {
    const result = await pinata.pinFileToIPFS(file, {
      pinataMetadata: { name: file.name },
      pinataOptions: { cidVersion: 0 }
    });
    return result.IpfsHash;
  } catch (error) {
    return null;
  }
}
Note: in the browser use the File object; in Node use a readable stream. Never commit API secrets to source control.
Error handling
Return null or display a friendly message on failure. Distinguish network errors from permission or key issues.
Security note
Store API keys in environment variables. When you cannot hide a secret in the client, proxy requests through a trusted backend.

screens.title: Storing CIDs on-chain: Solidity example
screens.subtitle: A minimal contract to hold a current image CID

narration.text: Storing a CID on-chain is straightforward: the data stored is a short string or bytes field that references off-chain content. The provided ImageStorage contract uses a public string currentImageCID and an owner-restricted setter. The constructor can initialize a default placeholder CID so the UI has something to display. Important practical notes: store the CID as string if you prefer readability and ease of use in higher-level libraries, or as bytes if you need to conserve a tiny amount of gas and handle encoding carefully. Access control is vital — in the example only the owner can change the CID, preventing arbitrary replacement. When your DApp calls setImageCID, make sure the caller is authorized and that the transaction is confirmed before assuming the new CID is available. Emit events when the CID changes so frontends can listen and refresh automatically. This pattern keeps on-chain storage minimal while enabling immutable references to heavy content on IPFS. Storing CIDs on-chain: Solidity example means keep a short string or bytes on-chain as a canonical reference to ipfs content; control updates and emit events for ui sync.. In practical terms, a minimal contract to hold a current image cid. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Minimal on-chain reference
keyIdea.text: Keep a short string or bytes on-chain as a canonical reference to IPFS content; control updates and emit events for UI sync.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Solidity Storage
ImageStorage contract
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract ImageStorage {
    string public currentImageCID;
    address public owner;

    event ImageCIDUpdated(address indexed updater, string newCID);

    constructor() {
        owner = msg.sender;
        currentImageCID = "QmUNLLsPekqG2qK1V2s6rYf2A1C1C1C1C1C1C1C1C"; // Default placeholder CID
    }

    function setImageCID(string memory _newCID) public {
        require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can set CID");
        currentImageCID = _newCID;
        emit ImageCIDUpdated(msg.sender, _newCID);
    }
}
The contract stores only a small string and emits an event when updated so the frontend can react to changes.
Practical tip
Use events to update the UI instead of polling. Keep storage minimal to reduce gas across transactions.
Access control
Restrict who can change CIDs to avoid malicious replacements; the example uses a simple owner pattern.

screens.title: DApp integration: Uploader component and contract interaction
screens.subtitle: End-to-end architecture: browser, pinning service, and smart contract

narration.text: This architecture slide ties the uploader UI, pinning service, and smart contract into a single flow you can implement. The browser holds the uploader component, which validates files and either calls a backend or a pinning SDK directly. The pinning service returns a CID which the browser then formats as ipfs://CID and sends in a transaction to the ImageStorage contract. The contract updates currentImageCID and emits an event. The front end listens for that event or fetches the contract state to display the updated image via an IPFS gateway. Important design decisions include whether to call the pinning service directly from the browser — which requires careful handling of A P I keys or token-based proxies — or to route uploads via a backend that stores secrets. Another choice is how to present fallback gateways: allow custom gateways in settings so users can reduce reliance on a single public gateway. Events provide a robust synchronization mechanism, and pinning ensures persistent availability. This architecture minimizes on-chain storage, maintains verifiability with CIDs, and balances decentralization with reliability. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › IPFSUploader
Starter component notes
The component initializes the contract, listens for events, handles file selection, uploads to Pinata, and updates the contract. It also shows status and errors for the user.
// Excerpt from IPFSUploader component
const pinata = pinataApiKey && pinataSecretApiKey ? new pinataSDK(pinataApiKey, pinataSecretApiKey) : null;

const handleUploadAndSetCID = async (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  if (!selectedFile || !pinata || !contract || !signer) return;

  setIsUploading(true);
  try {
    const result = await pinata.pinFileToIPFS(selectedFile, { pinataMetadata: { name: selectedFile.name }, pinataOptions: { cidVersion: 0 } });
    const newCID = result.IpfsHash;
    const tx = await contract.setImageCID(newCID);
    await tx.wait();
  } catch (err) {
    // Handle errors and user rejection
  } finally {
    setIsUploading(false);
  }
};
Always provide clear feedback: uploading, transaction pending, transaction confirmed. Use events to update UI state automatically.
Error modes
Handle API key misconfiguration, user transaction rejection, and network failures separately to help debugging.
UI verification
After confirmation, show the image via getIPFSGatewayURL(cid) and clear the file input so users know the process completed.

screens.title: CID Versions and Compatibility
screens.subtitle: Why CID v0 and v1 matter and what to watch for

narration.text: IPFS supports different CID versions, commonly v0 and v1. The difference affects encoding and interoperability: older tools and gateways may expect v0 CIDs, while some newer tools prefer v1 for multibase and multicodec features. The chapter notes that Pinata and similar tools allow specifying cidVersion when pinning. The practical implication is to be consistent across your toolchain. If you store a CID from one version in a contract but later use a tool that expects another encoding, retrieval or matching may appear to fail even though the underlying content is identical. A common confusion is to assume all CIDs are interchangeable. They are content-equivalent only if they represent the same underlying content, but encoding differences can create mismatches in tooling. When you design your workflow, standardize the CID version (or support both) and document it for integration points. This avoids subtle bugs during retrieval and makes your DApp more robust when working with multiple pinning services or gateways. CID Versions and Compatibility means choose and document a cid version for your dapp; mismatched encodings can cause interoperability surprises even for identical content.. In practical terms, why cid v0 and v1 matter and what to watch for. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Be consistent with CID versions
keyIdea.text: Choose and document a CID version for your DApp; mismatched encodings can cause interoperability surprises even for identical content.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › CID Versions
CID v0 vs v1
CID versions differ in encoding and feature support. Pinning options often let you pick a version; be deliberate about it.
v0
Widespread support and legacy tools.
v1

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety notes
screens.subtitle: Pinning, gateway reliance, content moderation, and large file handling

narration.text: This lesson summarizes typical pitfalls and recommended safeguards. First, don't assume IPFS alone ensures persistence; content must be pinned by one or more nodes to avoid garbage collection. If important files are unpinned, they may disappear from public gateways. Second, relying solely on public gateways is convenient but introduces a centralized access point; include fallback gateways or allow user-configured gateways. Third, consider content moderation: a CID proves immutability but not appropriateness or safety. Your DApp should still validate or moderate user-submitted content if required. Fourth, large files can be slow to retrieve; optimize assets before upload and consider chunking or progressive delivery. Fifth, guard secrets: A P I keys for pinning providers must not be committed to client code. Use a backend proxy when necessary. Finally, monitor availability: pinning services help but also consider redundancy by pinning with multiple providers or running a dedicated node. These precautions help prevent unexpected downtime and legal or UX issues in production. Mistakes that break availability
  • Assuming an uploaded CID remains available without pinning.
  • Exposing pinning API secrets in client-side code.
  • Storing large binaries on-chain instead of references.
  • Using a single public gateway as the only retrieval path.
Mitigations

Moderation note
A CID guarantees immutability but not that the content is appropriate. Implement moderation policies for user-generated content if necessary.

screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's wrap up the essential concepts. First, decentralized storage complements blockchains: store large files off-chain and keep compact, verifiable references on-chain. Second, IPFS uses content addressing; CIDs are cryptographic fingerprints of content and guarantee immutability. Third, pinning services are necessary for persistence: without pins, content may be garbage-collected and become unavailable. Keep these three ideas in mind when designing a DApp that needs media or large metadata. They determine whether your application is cost-effective, verifiable, and resilient. Finally, adopt practical safeguards: use environment variables for keys, prefer a pinning service or multiple providers for production, and emit events from contracts to synchronize your UI. These practices make your DApp reliable while keeping it aligned with decentralized principles. Content Addressing
Data is identified by its cryptographic hash (CID), not location.
IPFS
A peer-to-peer file system that serves content by CID from any node that has it.
Pinning
Pinning prevents garbage collection and ensures content stays available over time.
Summary takeaway

Use IPFS for heavy content, store small CIDs on-chain, and rely on pinning services or nodes for persistence to build resilient DApps.

narration.text: These three compact reminders are practical anchors for daily development. First, remember that a CID is the canonical fingerprint of content and that identical content yields identical CIDs. Second, pinning guarantees persistence; without pinning, content may vanish from public gateways. Third, store only the CID on-chain and keep heavy assets in IPFS to minimize gas and maintain verifiability. Keep these in mind when you build uploader UI, choose a pinning provider, and design contract interfaces. They will help you avoid costly mistakes and make your DApp easier to maintain and reason about.
